UC Berkeley Major Migration

One page, three passes over the same student flows, in rising order of depth: a flow diagram tracing each entering class from intended major to declared major to degree (including no degree at all); a role grid showing the measured role each department plays, cohort by cohort; and a department scatter plot placing every department by how much of its intenders’ traffic it keeps and how much of its population it imports — with time, admit rates, and demographics layered on.

UC Berkeley major migration · intended → declared → degree

Intended, Declared, Degree

Entering students traced through three stages — what they intended on the application, what they declared, and the division that finally granted their degree, including the students who left with no degree at all, so the right-hand edge is a full partition of the entering cohort. Band width is people. Hover a band for its year-by-year history and the department flows inside it; click a stage-1 or stage-3 node to trace its students through all three stages; drag a node up or down to reorder its column.

UC Berkeley major migration · structural roles, measured

Department Migration Roles

Departments play measurable roles in the migration system — some keep their intenders, some are built on arrivals, some feed one corridor. Start with the role grid just below: which role each department plays, cohort by cohort, with the roles found by clustering the flow data itself. Then move to the department scatter plot beneath it — every department placed by how much of its intenders’ traffic it keeps (→ right) and how much of its population is imported (↑ up), with each cohort’s trail, decade-long paths, and admit rates drawn as rings around the dots.

Right = keeps the students who intended it. Up = built on imports (or, on the concentration axis: its leavers funnel into one corridor). Dot area = people. Ring = the admit rate of the department’s college (arc length = the rate). Tail = the previous four cohorts. Hatched = partial data; hollow = recording artifact. Click a dot to pin it — the panel on the right fills with its numbers.
